content: 1. Certain arguments were identified that oppose the recommendation to lower trans-fatty acid (TFA) intake. 2. Recommendation 2 was classified as conditional because, while evidence from various study types in systematic reviews suggests that reducing TFA intake to less than 1% of total energy intake is associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), and coronary heart disease, the evidence is less robust compared to higher TFA intakes (greater than 1% of total energy intake). This results in lower confidence in the findings, as the overall certainty of evidence is low. 3. No adverse effects or mitigating factors were identified that would argue against reducing TFA intake to less than 1% of total energy intake. 4. A conservative approach was adopted, leading to a conditional recommendation. 5. Recommendation 3 is based on very low-certainty evidence for replacing TFA with polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and moderate-certainty evidence for replacing TFA with monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) derived from plant sources. 6. Evidence supporting this recommendation comes from two systematic reviews that analyzed the effects of lower versus higher TFA intake through replacement nutrient analysis. These reviews found that lower TFA intake reduced the risk of all-cause mortality, CVDs, coronary heart disease, and type 2 diabetes. 7. Specific findings from the reviews include: In prospective observational studies, replacing TFA with PUFAs was associated with a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes (very low-certainty evidence). Replacing TFA with plant-based MUFAs was associated with a reduced risk of all-cause mortality, CVDs, and coronary heart disease (moderate-certainty evidence). In randomized controlled trials (RCTs), replacing TFA with PUFAs, MUFAs, or carbohydrates resulted in reductions in LDL cholesterol (high-certainty evidence) and overall improvements in blood lipid profiles. The greatest reduction in LDL cholesterol was observed with PUFAs, followed by MUFAs, and then carbohydrates. 8. Recommendation 3 was classified as conditional because evidence for disease outcomes comes primarily from a limited number of observational studies, while most of the evidence is derived from RCTs using LDL cholesterol as an outcome. 9. The evidence for LDL cholesterol is of high certainty. However, while LDL cholesterol is a well-established biomarker for assessing the effects of interventions on CVD risk and is considered a causal factor for atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease, it is not a direct manifestation or confirmation of disease. Therefore, a conservative approach was taken, leading to a conditional recommendation. 10. The recommendation to replace TFA with PUFAs or plant-based MUFAs does not exclude replacing TFA with carbohydrates. Replacement with carbohydrates significantly lowered LDL cholesterol in RCTs assessing blood lipids. However, PUFAs and MUFAs had greater effects on LDL cholesterol when used as replacements for TFA. Additionally, replacing TFA with plant-based MUFAs reduced the risk of coronary heart disease and all-cause mortality in prospective observational studies. 11. Limited evidence suggests that replacing TFA with carbohydrates of unspecified composition also reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes. However, replacing TFA with free sugars or refined carbohydrates, as described by study authors, has little effect on the risk of coronary heart disease. Therefore, a conclusive interpretation of the results for carbohydrate replacement of TFA in the analyses supporting these recommendations was not possible. 12. Replacing TFA with saturated fatty acids (SFAs) did not improve disease outcomes or blood lipids in the two systematic reviews. SFAs are therefore not a preferred replacement for TFA. 13. To facilitate implementation of this recommendation, TFA replacement can be achieved through PUFAs, MUFAs, or a combination of the two. 14. This guidance on replacement nutrients is relevant for a state of energy balance, where total energy consumed is balanced by total energy expended. In cases of energy balance, when the intake of one nutrient is reduced, the resulting energy deficit must be compensated for by the intake of another nutrient. In cases of positive energy balance, where a reduction in total energy intake is desired, TFA intake may be reduced partially or entirely without the need for a replacement nutrient. 15. Because no relevant studies on TFA intake in children were identified in a systematic review, the recommendations for children are based on extrapolation of results obtained from reviews conducted in adults. 16. These recommendations do not preclude the consumption of specific foods. However, foods containing high levels of industrially produced TFA should largely be avoided. 17. The results from reviews conducted in adults were not downgraded for indirectness when assessing evidence via the GRADE framework, as there is no evidence to suggest that the physiological effects of reducing or increasing TFA on disease risk and mortality would differ significantly between adults and children. 18. Industrially produced TFA are the predominant source of dietary TFA in many populations. Foods such as doughnuts, cookies, crackers, pies, and other pre-packaged snacks are common sources. Although current intakes of ruminant TFA are generally low, ruminant TFA may become the predominant dietary source of TFA in populations where industrially produced TFA are being phased out of the food supply. 19. High intake of industrially produced TFA is strongly associated with an increased risk of coronary heart disease and related mortality. Few studies have identified an association between ruminant TFA intake and CVDs; however, ruminant TFA intake in most study populations has been very low. 20. Efforts to reduce industrially produced TFA in the food supply received a boost in 2018 when their elimination was identified as a priority target in the WHO 13th General Programme of Work. The WHO REPLACE action package was launched in 2018 to help countries eliminate industrially produced TFA from their food supplies. 21. The updated WHO recommendations for SFA and TFA intake aim to provide evidence-informed guidance to policymakers and program managers to address SFA and TFA intake in their populations through various policy actions and public health interventions. 22. Updating the WHO recommendations for SFA and TFA intake is a critical component of WHO’s efforts to implement the noncommunicable disease (NCD) agenda and achieve the “triple billion” targets set by the 13th General Programme of Work, including improving the health and well-being of 1 billion more people. 23. The recommendations also support the implementation of commitments from the UN high-level meetings on NCD prevention and control, the WHO Global Action Plan for NCDs, and the recommendations of the High-Level Commission on Ending Childhood Obesity. 24. Despite longstanding dietary advice to limit SFA intake and focused efforts to reduce TFA intake at the population level, SFA intake remains high in many parts of the world. While efforts to reduce industrially produced TFA in the food supply have led to decreased intake in some countries, the global average intake of TFA in 2010 exceeded the population nutrient intake goal of 1% of total energy intake established by WHO. 25. The updated guidance reflects new data and analyses, which have led to differing interpretations and conclusions regarding the role of SFA intake in health, particularly in relation to CVD risk. The debate continues about whether current evidence supports a link between SFA intake and CVDs and whether efforts to limit SFA intake as a means of reducing CVD risk are warranted. 26. There is increasing scientific consensus about the adverse health effects of industrially produced TFA intake. However, discussions continue regarding the role of ruminant TFA consumption in the development of NCDs. 27. The updated WHO guidance on SFA and TFA intake is part of a broader effort to update population nutrient intake goals for the prevention of NCDs. The focus of this guideline is on the health effects of SFA and TFA intake.
